lesson.title: Short Circuit: The Path of Least Resistance
lesson.summary: A short circuit is an unintended near zero resistance path that lets current surge far beyond what the circuit was designed to carry, which is why it is dangerous rather than harmless.
lesson.body:
If an open circuit is a broken path, a short circuit is almost the opposite problem: an extra path appears where one should not exist, and that path has almost no resistance at all. A short happens when two points in a circuit that are meant to be separated by some resistance get connected directly instead, by a stray wire, a solder bridge, frayed insulation, or a failed component. Current, always looking for the path that offers the least opposition, rushes through that low resistance shortcut instead of following its intended route through the rest of the circuit.

Ohm's law explains why this is dangerous rather than merely inconvenient. Current equals voltage divided by resistance, so as the resistance in the denominator shrinks toward zero, the current in that branch grows very large for any nonzero voltage. In a truly ideal short with exactly zero resistance and an ideal voltage source, the math predicts infinite current, which of course cannot really happen. In real circuits, the current is limited by whatever small resistance remains, most importantly the internal resistance of the source itself and the resistance of the wires, and that limited but still very large current is what melts insulation, overheats wires, and can start fires.

This is why real batteries and power supplies are modeled as an ideal source in series with a small internal resistance, rather than as a perfect source with zero resistance. That internal resistance is usually irrelevant during normal operation because it is tiny compared to the load resistance, but during a short circuit, the load resistance vanishes and the internal resistance becomes the only thing standing between the source and a runaway current.

Consider a 12 volt battery with an internal resistance of 0.5 ohms. Under normal use with a 6 ohm load resistor, the total resistance is 6 ohms plus 0.5 ohms, or 6.5 ohms, giving a current of 12 divided by 6.5, about 1.85 amps, a perfectly reasonable value. Now suppose the output terminals get shorted together by a dropped tool or a damaged cable, bypassing the 6 ohm load entirely. The only resistance left in the loop is the internal 0.5 ohms, so the short circuit current is 12 volts divided by 0.5 ohms, which is 24 amps, exactly thirteen times the normal operating current. That surge is exactly the kind of event that fuses and circuit breakers exist to detect and interrupt before wires overheat.

Short circuits are the reason electrical codes require fuses, breakers, and proper insulation, and they are why engineers calculate worst case short circuit current when designing protection systems. Understanding a short as a resistance path that has collapsed toward zero, rather than as some mysterious electrical event, makes it much easier to predict how a circuit will misbehave and how to protect against it.
